title: iPhone Emojis: Copy & Paste Apple Emojis
meta_description: Copy popular iPhone (Apple) emojis and learn how iOS emojis really work — they share the same Unicode as Android, only the artwork differs.
hero_tagline: Copy popular Apple (iOS) emojis and understand how they actually work. The short version: iPhone emojis are the same Unicode characters as Android emojis. Only the artwork is different. Click any emoji to copy it instantly.
intro: People search for “iPhone emojis” for two reasons: to copy the familiar Apple-style emojis, and to figure out why an emoji looks one way on their iPhone and another way on a friend’s Android. This page does both. Below you can copy the most-used iOS emojis grouped by category, and the explainers clear up the single most misunderstood thing about emoji: iPhone and Android emojis are the same characters. There is no separate “Apple emoji” code and “Android emoji” code. Every emoji is one Unicode code point, shared by every platform. Apple, Google, Samsung, Microsoft, WhatsApp and Twitter each draw their own picture for that code point, which is why the same 😂 can look subtly (or wildly) different depending on the device showing it.

editorial_sections.h2: iPhone vs Android emojis: same characters, different artwork
paragraphs: Think of an emoji like a letter of the alphabet. The letter “A” is the same letter whether it is set in Helvetica or Times New Roman: only the font changes how it looks. Emoji work exactly the same way. The emoji “Face with Tears of Joy” is the single Unicode code point U+1F602 on every device on earth. When you type it on an iPhone, your phone sends that code point, not the Apple picture. The receiving device then looks up U+1F602 in its own emoji font and draws its own version.
That is why your messages are never garbled across platforms: the text is identical. What you are seeing is two designers’ interpretations of the same idea:

So when you copy an emoji from this page, you are copying the character, not Apple’s picture. Paste it into an iPhone and you’ll see the Apple design; paste it into an Android phone and you’ll see Google’s design. The meaning carries; the look depends on the reader’s device.

editorial_sections.h2: How to get the latest iPhone emojis
paragraphs: New emojis are not a download you grab on their own: they arrive bundled inside an iOS update. Each year the Unicode Consortium approves a new batch of emoji, and Apple has shipped each year’s set in a spring point update in recent years (iOS 16.4, 17.4 and 18.4 each carried one). To make sure you have the newest characters and the freshest artwork, open Settings → General → Software Update and install the latest iOS.

This also explains the dreaded blank box. If you send a brand-new emoji to someone on an older OS, their device may not have artwork for that code point yet, so it renders as a featureless box (▯) or a question mark. The character is perfectly valid: their phone just needs an update to draw it. Updating iOS (or Android) fills in the missing pictures. For the wider picture, see why a character turns into a box.

editorial_sections.h2: Skin tones are part of the character too
paragraphs: When you pick a skin tone for a hand or person emoji on iPhone, you are not choosing a setting: you are appending a second Unicode character (a skin-tone modifier, U+1F3FB through U+1F3FF) to the base emoji. Because it is just more text, that tone travels with the emoji to Android and everywhere else. The 👋🏽 you send keeps its medium tone on the other device; only the drawing style changes. This is the same principle as the rest of the page: it’s all standard Unicode, shared across platforms.

faq.q: Are iPhone emojis different from Android emojis?
faq.a: Not as characters. Every emoji is a single Unicode code point (or sequence) that is identical on iPhone, Android, Windows, and the web. What differs is the artwork: Apple draws its own emoji font, Google draws another for Android, and Samsung and Microsoft have their own. So 😂 is the exact same character everywhere, it just looks slightly different depending on which device renders it.

faq.q: Why do my emojis look different on Android than on iPhone?
faq.a: Because each platform ships its own emoji font (the set of pictures). When you send an emoji from an iPhone, you send the Unicode code point, not the Apple picture. The receiving Android phone looks up that same code point in Google’s emoji font and draws its own version. Nothing is lost or mistranslated: you are seeing two artists’ interpretations of the same character.

faq.q: How do I get the newest iPhone emojis?
faq.a: New emojis arrive with iOS updates, not from a separate download. Apple has shipped each year’s approved Unicode emoji set in a spring iOS point update in recent years (iOS 16.4, 17.4 and 18.4). Go to Settings → General → Software Update and install the latest iOS to get the newest emoji artwork and any brand-new characters.

faq.q: Can I copy iPhone emojis on a computer or Android phone?
faq.a: Yes. Because emojis are plain Unicode text, you can copy any emoji on this page from any device and paste it anywhere: Windows, Mac, Android, or the web. The character will travel correctly; it will simply be drawn in whatever emoji font the destination device uses, which may not be Apple’s.

faq.q: Why does an emoji show up as a blank box or question mark?
faq.a: A blank box (▯) or question mark means the device’s emoji font does not yet include that character, usually because the operating system is older than the emoji. The character itself is valid Unicode. Updating the OS (for example, installing the latest iOS) adds the missing artwork and the box becomes a proper emoji.

faq.q: Is there an “Apple font” that makes Android show iPhone emojis?
faq.a: Not officially. Apple’s emoji font (Apple Color Emoji) is licensed for Apple devices, so Android does not legally ship it. Some third-party keyboards or rooted-device font swaps imitate the look, but the reliable, cross-platform fact is that the underlying characters are already identical: only the rendering differs.
